text: Potential energy diagrams and stability. Gravitational potential energy. Graphs are a good way to obtain useful information about a dynamical behavior of a system. Let's consider a one-dimensional system whose potential energy is known, U of Y equals Mgy. We can use this potential energy function for an object in freefall near the Earth's surface neglecting air resistance. The mechanical energy of the object is conserved, E equals K plus U equals constant. We choose Y to represent the vertical height relative to the ground, Y equals zero. The total energy is divided between kinetic and potential energy as the object's height changes. Solving for Y gives Y is less than or equal to E over Mgy equals Y max. At the maximum height, the kinetic energy and speed are zero. If the object were initially traveling upward, its velocity would go to zero, and Y max would be a turning point in the motion. E equals K of V sub zero equals one-half M v sub zero to the power of two. V sub zero equals plus or minus square root of two E over M. The maximum speed plus or minus V sub zero gives the initial velocity necessary to reach the maximum height Y max, and negative V sub zero represents the final velocity after falling from Y max. Potential energy of a spring. Consider a mass spring system, the figure, on a frictionless stationary horizontal surface so that gravity and the normal contact force do no work and can be ignored. This is like a one-dimensional system whose mechanical energy E is a constant and whose potential energy U of X equals one-half K X squared with respect to zero energy at zero displacement from the springs unstretched length X equals zero. You can deduce the physically allowable range of motion, as well as the maximum values of distance and speed from the limits on the kinetic energy, zero is less than or equal to K is less than or equal to E. We can find two turning points when K equals zero and U equals E for the elastic spring potential energy. X max equals plus or minus square root of two E over K. The glider's motion in Fig A is confined to the region between the turning points. Minus X max is less than or equal to X, which is less than or equal to X max. This is true for any positive value of E because the potential energy is unbounded with respect to X. For this reason, U of X is called an infinite potential well. At the bottom of the potential well, X equals zero and U equals zero, while the kinetic energy is a maximum, K equals E and V max equals plus or minus square root of two E over M. From the slope of this potential energy curve, Fig B, you can deduce information about the force on the glider and its acceleration. The slope, force and acceleration are all zero when X equals zero, so this is an equilibrium point. The negative of the slope on either side of the equilibrium point gives a force pointing back to the equilibrium point, i.e. F equals plus or minus KX, so the equilibrium is termed stable, and the force is called a restoring force. If the force on either side of an equilibrium point has a direction that is the same as the direction of position change, i.e. pointing away from the equilibrium point, the equilibrium is termed unstable. A stable point occurs when U of X has a relative minimum, while an unstable point occurs when U of X has a relative maximum. This should be intuitive because a ball rolls downhill into a valley.
